title: What is an HTTP Parameter Pollution (HPP) attack: supplying a parameter multiple times (`?role=user&role=admin`) so different layers (gateway, framework, backend) disagree on which value wins, bypassing validation/authorization: and how do you remediate it (reject or canonicalize duplicate params, validate against a strict schema, be explicit about first-vs-last-wins semantics)?
shortTitle: What is an HTTP Parameter Pollution (HPP) attack and how do you remediate it
keyPoints: HPP exploits the lack of a universal rule for which occurrence of a duplicate parameter wins in HTTP.
Java Servlet getParameter returns the first value, Spring may bind the first, but a gateway in another language may take the last.
The attacker crafts a request so the security layer reads the safe value while the business layer reads the dangerous one.
The strongest fix is rejecting duplicate single-valued parameters outright with a 400 Bad Request.
Canonicalization (first-wins or last-wins, documented and uniform) removes ambiguity if duplicates must be accepted.
Strict schema validation with typed DTOs and enums prevents polluted values from reaching the service layer.

s1_definition.oneliner: HPP is sending the same parameter twice so your security layer and your business layer read different values and the attacker slips through the gap.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **HTTP Parameter Pollution (HPP)** – an attack where the same parameter name is supplied more than once in a request, e.g. `?role=user&role=admin`.
- **No universal rule** – HTTP does not define which occurrence wins; Java Servlet takes the first, some gateways take the last, Spring can return an array.
- **Exploit** – the security filter reads one occurrence while the business layer reads another, bypassing validation or authorization.
- **Remediation** – reject duplicates with 400, canonicalize to one deterministic value, or validate against a strict typed schema.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh fills a bank withdrawal slip but writes the amount twice: 5,000 at the top and 500,000 at the bottom. The security guard at the door glances at the top and sees a small amount, so he waves Rajesh through. But the cashier at the counter reads the bottom line and pays out 500,000. Two people looked at the same form and saw different numbers. HPP is exactly this: the same field sent twice so the guard and the cashier disagree.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  HPP Attack Flow:

  Attacker sends: ?role=user&role=admin

  ┌───────────────────┐    reads LAST → "user" → OK
  │  API Gateway       │
  └────────┬──────────┘
           │
           ▼
  ┌───────────────────┐    reads FIRST → "admin" → executes!
  │  Backend Service   │
  └───────────────────┘

  Fix: reject duplicates at the first layer

  ┌───────────────────┐    detects duplicate → 400 Bad Request
  │  HPP Filter        │
  └───────────────────┘    (never reaches business logic)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
HTTP Parameter Pollution is an attack where the same parameter is supplied more than once in a request, exploiting the fact that there is no universal rule for which occurrence wins. Java Servlet's `getParameter` returns the first value, Spring may bind the first, and a gateway in another language may take the last. When the security layer reads one occurrence and the business layer reads another, the attacker bypasses authorization.

The strongest remediation is to reject duplicates outright: if a single-valued parameter appears more than once, return 400 before any business logic runs. If duplicates must be accepted, canonicalize to a single deterministic value and document whether first-wins or last-wins, making every layer use the same rule. On top of that, validate with typed DTOs and enums so polluted values fail binding.

At National Bank of India, the transfer API was vulnerable because the gateway read the last `accountType` value and the backend read the first. A customer sent `accountType=savings&accountType=current` and bypassed the savings transfer limit by fooling the gateway into treating it as a savings account while the backend processed it as current. The fix was an HPP filter that rejects any single-valued parameter sent twice, combined with strict enum binding.

The principle is that ambiguity is the vulnerability. Any time two components can interpret the same input differently, an attacker will engineer that difference. Eliminating the ambiguity by rejecting duplicates and validating at the boundary is the fix.

Remember one sentence: if a parameter that should appear once appears twice, reject it, because the gap between how two layers read it is the vulnerability.
